name: Royal purple
lede: Royal purple is a medium-dark blue-violet named for the dye that Roman custom reserved for the emperor, though the name has outlived any single recipe.

sections.title: A color kept for rulers
sections.body:
Roman custom kept purple for the highest offices. A general wore a purple and gold robe at his triumph, senators wore broad purple stripes on their tunics, and knights narrow ones [1]. Cicero and other writers of the first century BC and AD already spoke of *royal purple*, and by the time of Diocletian, in the early fourth century, it was tied to the emperor alone [1]. The physicist Livingstone adds a reason that has nothing to do with law: a purple object must absorb a narrow band of light, so purple objects are uncommon, and purple dyes were historically rare and costly [2].

By the fifteenth century the meaning had loosened. An early fifteenth-century French heraldic treatise called purple a mixture of all the other tinctures, and painters of the period disagreed on what to use for it, among mauve, wine color and mulberry [3].

sections.title: A name for new dyes
sections.body: The title was used again in 1522, when the Spanish emissary Gil Gonzales de Davila found pearls and a purple dye in the Nicoya area of Central America (today's Costa Rica) [4]. Finlay reports that the Spanish king called it New World Royal Purple and, perhaps remembering Rome, demanded exclusive use of it [4]. When de Menonville crushed a powdery insect on paper during his search for the cochineal insect, his account describes the result as a royal purple hue [5]. In both cases the phrase is used for a hue, not a single material.

sections.title: Which royal purple?
sections.body:
Paterson defines the term as simply a dark purple [6]. Our swatch, #7851A9, is a mid-tone blue-violet [7]. Ridgway's 1912 plate, as scanned, is a little duller at #69519A, and the xkcd survey's "royal purple" is a much darker #4B006E, about 19 units from ours [7]. Maerz and Paul recorded the name in English in 1661, and ISCC-NBS block 207 covers it [7].

Similar colors are [[purple]], [[violet]], [[imperial-purple]] and [[tyrian-purple]]. The last two carry the same ancient associations but are separate names in our data.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The name is better documented in texts than in paint. Our archive tool could not produce a stable count for this color, so no painting count is given here [7].
